sections.body_md:
A norm measures the size of a vector. Three rules define it. A nonzero vector has positive size. Scaling a vector by \(c\) scales the size by \(\lvert c \rvert\), so a negative scalar does not make the size negative. The triangle inequality says a sum is at most the sum of the sizes.

The usual \(\ell_p\) family all satisfy those rules. The 1-norm adds the absolute coordinates. The 2-norm is the ordinary Euclidean length. The infinity-norm keeps only the largest absolute coordinate. The general \(\ell_p\) norm takes the \(p\)-th root of the sum of \(p\)-th powers of the absolute coordinates. As \(p\) grows, that expression approaches the infinity-norm.

The unit ball, the set of vectors with norm at most 1, shows the difference in shape. The 1-norm ball is a diamond, the 2-norm ball is a disk, and the infinity-norm ball is a square. In finite dimension the shapes differ but the norms are equivalent: each is bounded by a constant times any other. The constants can grow with the dimension. Equivalence is not equality.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
For \(x \in \mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
\lVert x \rVert_1 = \sum_i \lvert x_i \rvert, \qquad
\lVert x \rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_i x_i^2}, \qquad
\lVert x \rVert_\infty = \max_i \lvert x_i \rvert.
\]
Useful comparisons are \(\lVert x \rVert_\infty \le \lVert x \rVert_2 \le \lVert x \rVert_1 \le \sqrt{n}\,\lVert x \rVert_2 \le n\,\lVert x \rVert_\infty\). The open ball of radius \(r\) about \(x\) is the strict inequality \(\lVert y - x \rVert < r\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Take \(x = (6, -8)\). The absolute coordinates are 6 and 8. Their sum is 14, so the 1-norm is the sum of absolutes 14. The Euclidean length is \(\sqrt{36+64} = \sqrt{100}\), so the length is 10. The larger absolute coordinate is 8, so the infinity-norm is 8.

The ratio of the 1-norm to the infinity-norm is \(14/8 = 1.75\). In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) that ratio cannot exceed 2, and this vector does not reach the bound because the two absolute coordinates are not equal. The 2-norm sits between them: \(8 < 10 < 14\).

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: A norm of a sum is not always the sum of the norms. That equality holds for the 1-norm only in special sign patterns, and for the 2-norm when the vectors are nonnegative multiples of one vector. Homogeneity uses the absolute value of the scalar. In infinite dimension, equivalence can fail; the finite-dimensional statement does not transfer unchanged. The unit ball of the infinity-norm is a square, not a disk, so drawing one ball for every norm misstates the geometry.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Cauchy-Schwarz is a statement about the 2-norm that comes from the dot product, and it is the step that proves the triangle inequality for that norm. Induced matrix norms measure how much a matrix can stretch a vector, using a vector norm in the definition. Open and closed sets are defined with balls of a norm, and equivalence of norms means they determine the same open sets.
